Integrators, OEMs and Channel Partners

Playbooklowob research

By Chris WellsFrom lowob RESEARCH · 25 August 2026 · 7-minute read · Distribution

In emerging tech the buyer already trusts someone else's hands; your job is to make those hands want to carry you, one partner at a time. Most technology spending already moves that way: Canalys estimated 70% of customer spending on technology, IT services and telecom services would go through partners in 2025. Do the first deployments yourself, productise the playbook into documents a partner can use, then work one partner's live deal to paid pilot before adding a second. Measure partner-sourced pipeline that reaches paid pilot, and nothing else.

The buyer already has suppliers

Part 8 made the case that when platforms are closed, distribution has to be built. In emerging tech the platforms are people. A utility, a port operator, a hospital group or a mine does not buy a robot, a sensor network or a verification layer from a startup. It buys from whoever already holds three things.

The relationship: an integrator or engineering firm that has been on site for years. The procurement vehicle: a framework agreement, an approved vendor list, a distributor already in the system. The liability: a managed service provider who answers the call at 3am and carries the insurance.

The scale of that structure is measurable in technology markets generally. Canalys, an analyst firm, forecast worldwide IT spending of $5.44 trillion in 2025 and estimated that 70% of it would go through partners, down from 71% in 2024 and 73% in 2023. Forrester's 2025 buyers' journey survey, cited in February 2026, found an average of nine people from outside the buying organisation involved in a purchase decision. Many of those outside voices are the integrators and advisers the buyer already pays.

You can fight that structure or use it. Fighting it means two-year sales cycles against a buyer who wants to say no. Using it means selling once to the partner and letting the partner sell many times.

What the partner believes

Part 2 asked for a belief per audience. The partner's belief is not your customer's belief. The customer wants risk retired. The partner wants three plainer things.

Margin: a deal that pays better than reselling what they already resell. Differentiation: something to say in a tender that the next integrator cannot say. No support burden: confidence that your product will not turn their engineers into your unpaid support desk.

If your pitch to a partner is the same deck you show customers, you have not done the work. Write the partner's belief as one sentence and put it in the claims register.

What a channel partner needs from you

Partners are not evaluating your technology. They are evaluating the cost of carrying it. Five things lower that cost.

What the partner needsWhat good looks likeWhat fails
A reference deploymentLive, with a customer who will take their callA pilot under NDA nobody can speak about
A certified integrationTested and documented with what the partner already installsRoadmap
TrainingA module their field and sales teams can complete, with a pass markA deck and a recorded webinar
Partner marginSurvives their cost of sale, which carries travel, site time and bid costYour direct discount, relabelled
A support pathA service level, an escalation route and a named person on your sideA shared inbox

Miss any one and the partner will sign your agreement and sell what they already know. Partner channel design sets out how to define the partner's role in the sale and pay each type accordingly.

Direct first, channel second

The temptation is to recruit partners before the product is stable, because partners look like a multiplier. They multiply only once there is something repeatable to multiply.

Do the first deployments yourself. Part 33's design partners are where the playbook comes from. You learn the site-survey questions, the installation sequence, the failure modes, the commissioning test, and what the customer calls the thing you sell. Write all of it down as you go.

Then productise the playbook. Installation guide, commissioning checklist, training module, support runbook, pricing sheet with partner margin. That document set is what you hand a partner. Without it you are asking them to learn at their own cost.

Partners multiply only once there is something repeatable to multiply.

OEM, embedded and platform programmes

Two other routes sit beside the channel.

OEM or embedded deals put your technology inside someone else's product. A perception module in a robotics platform, a verification layer in an identity product, a control algorithm in a battery system. In our experience these are slow to close, often eighteen months or more, sticky once live and lower margin than direct, and the reach can be larger than anything you could build. Price them as licences or per-unit royalties. Protect your right to sell direct and to serve other OEMs, and write down in advance which accounts each route owns. Channel conflict, and how to manage it covers the rules that stop an OEM and your direct team from bidding against each other.

Ecosystem and platform programmes are distribution with a badge. Cloud marketplaces, chip-vendor partner programmes, robotics platform ecosystems, standards-body member lists. They open procurement vehicles, co-marketing and sometimes co-selling. They rarely close deals on their own. Treat them as a channel to partners, not a channel to customers.

The procurement value is real and growing. Canalys projected in August 2024 that sales through hyperscaler cloud marketplaces would grow from $16 billion in 2023 to $85 billion by 2028, and that more than half would flow through the channel by 2027, using partner private offer programmes from AWS, Microsoft and Google Cloud. A marketplace listing lets a buyer spend committed cloud budget; a partner private offer lets the integrator keep its margin on that spend. Marketplace listings for B2B sellers and co-selling with platforms cover how each works.

The trap, and the measure

The trap is ten signed partners who do nothing. The partner agreement costs nothing to sign and nothing to ignore. A logo slide of integrators is not a channel.

The industry is moving the other way on volume. Forrester's 2025 partner ecosystem marketing survey found most vendors expected their ecosystems to grow in number of partners across every type, and 67% expected indirect revenue to grow by more than 30%. More partners raise the risk that each one gets less attention. Depth beats count.

Pick one partner with a live deal in front of them and a named owner inside their business who is paid on that deal. Work that deal with them to paid pilot. Then do it again with the same partner before you add a second.

Measure partner-sourced pipeline that reaches paid pilot. Not partners signed, not partner-registered leads, not joint webinars. One number, reported monthly alongside the direct equivalent. Where partners register deals, deal registration rules decide who is credited and protected.

StageWhat countsWhat does not
RecruitedNamed owner, live deal identifiedSigned agreement
EnabledTraining passed, integration certifiedDeck sent
SellingPartner-sourced paid pilotRegistered lead
ScalingSecond paid pilot, same partnerSecond partner

The checklist

ItemDone when
Partner beliefWritten as one sentence and in the claims register
PlaybookFirst deployments done direct; the document set exists
First partnerOne partner has a live deal, a named owner and a commission on it
MarginTested against the partner's real cost of sale
SupportService levels and an escalation route in place
MeasurePartner-sourced pipeline to paid pilot is the only channel metric reported

lowob takeaways

  • Sell to whoever holds the relationship, the vehicle and the liability. Most technology spend already moves through partners.
  • Write the partner's belief, not the customer's. Margin, differentiation and no support burden.
  • Go direct first, then hand over a document set. Partners will not learn your product at their own cost.
  • Treat marketplaces and programmes as routes to partners. They open procurement; they rarely close deals.
  • Measure paid pilots, not signatures. Depth with one partner beats a logo slide of ten.

Common questions

How do emerging tech startups sell through channel partners?

Sell once to the partner and let the partner sell many times. Give them a live reference deployment, a certified integration, training with a pass mark, a margin that survives their cost of sale, and a support path with a service level.

When should a startup start recruiting channel partners?

Only once there is something repeatable to multiply. Do the first deployments yourself, write the playbook down, then productise it before handing it to a partner.

What metric should I use to measure channel partner performance?

Partner-sourced pipeline that reaches paid pilot, reported monthly alongside the direct equivalent. Not partners signed, partner-registered leads or joint webinars.

How should OEM or embedded technology deals be priced?

Price them as licences or per-unit royalties, and protect your right to sell direct and to serve other OEMs, with written rules on which accounts each route owns.
